title: SHE HID THEM UNDER THE FLAX—BUT GOD WAS HIDING SOMETHING BIGGER
paragraphs:
SHE HID THEM UNDER THE FLAX—BUT GOD WAS HIDING SOMETHING BIGGER
Rahab thought she was hiding two hunted men on her roof. She could not have known that, in that terrifying night, God was writing a former prostitute into the story that would eventually lead to Jesus Christ.
There were footsteps outside her door.
Not neighbors coming to borrow something. Not customers wandering through the night. These were the king’s men.
Somebody had seen the strangers enter Rahab’s house.
And somewhere above them, on the flat roof of a house built into Jericho’s defenses, two Israelite spies were lying beneath stalks of flax.
Imagine Rahab hearing the voices below while knowing that the men they wanted were only a short distance away.
One stalk shifting beneath a nervous hand.
And everything could have ended differently.
Joshua 2:6 preserves the scene in Hebrew:
Vehi he‘elatam haggagah, vattitmenem bepishtei ha‘etz...
She had taken them up to the roof and hidden them among the stalks of flax.
And underneath it were two men carrying information connected with Israel’s entrance into the land God had promised.
But the most extraordinary thing happening on that roof was not that two spies were hidden.
It was what was happening inside Rahab.
She had heard what Israel's God had done.
She had heard about the sea.
She had heard about the kings who had fallen.
But Rahab did something with it.
“I know that the LORD has given you the land.”
Then comes one of the most astonishing confessions in the chapter:
"כִּי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל וְעַל־הָאָרֶץ מִתָּחַת"
Ki YHWH Eloheikhem hu Elohim bashamayim mimma‘al ve‘al-ha’aretz mittakhat.
The LORD your God—He is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath.
Not from someone raised inside Israel’s covenant community.
The woman Scripture introduced as a prostitute.
That is where this story stops being merely ancient history and starts getting uncomfortably close to us.
Because some of us know what it feels like to have one word attached to our identity.
Maybe nobody says the word anymore.
Maybe people have forgotten what you did.
Maybe you learned how to smile in church while privately remembering a version of yourself you desperately wish had never existed.
And Rahab’s story whispers something dangerous to shame:
Your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your final chapter.
That is part of what makes her story so powerful.
Joshua 2 introduces her plainly. She is Rahab, the prostitute.
The Bible does not need to pretend her past never happened in order to demonstrate what grace can do with a human life.
And Christianity does not proclaim that sinners save themselves by becoming respectable enough for God.
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
He lived the righteousness we could not produce.
He bore sin at the cross.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something shame could never manufacture:
Rahab's story is not the Gospel itself.
But her story points beautifully toward the kind of God revealed fully in the Gospel—a God whose grace reaches people whom respectable society might have already reduced to their history.
And here is something easy to miss.
Rahab herself says that they had heard what the LORD had done.
But hearing about God is not the same thing as trusting God.
Fear alone did not save Rahab.
Information alone did not save Rahab.
Centuries later, Hebrews reaches backward through Israel's history and refuses to forget her:
“By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace.”
Not “because she had a clean history.”
James remembers her too, pointing to her reception of the messengers and sending them away by another route as evidence of living, active faith.

The Bible does not tell Christians to imitate every morally complicated detail of Rahab's conduct that night. The New Testament specifically highlights her faith and the actions flowing from it—receiving the messengers and sending them safely onward.
There were soldiers at the door.
That is where faith becomes painfully real.
It is easy to say you believe when belief costs nothing.
It is different when obedience threatens your comfort.
When telling the truth costs money.
When abandoning a secret sin means killing the version of yourself you have been feeding for years.
When you finally have to decide whether Jesus is merely someone you admire...
She was physically inside Jericho, but her allegiance was changing.
Her address had not changed yet.
And somebody reading this understands that feeling.
You are still surrounded by the same environment.
Still living in the same neighborhood.
Still carrying consequences from old decisions.
Still waking up inside circumstances that have not miraculously disappeared.
Yet something inside you has changed.
Sin does not taste the same anymore.
The things you once justified now grieve you.
The life you once defended now exhausts you.
You are beginning to realize that repentance is not God stealing your life.
It is Christ rescuing you from the life that was destroying you.
Rahab could hear Jericho preparing for survival.
Yet she had come to believe that Jericho's walls could not save her.
And Rahab had somehow realized the most important truth in the city:
The wall everyone trusted was doomed.
You can build walls around your life too.
Anything can become a wall when we ask it to give us what only God can give.
And one day every false refuge fails.
Suddenly this woman whose life might have once revolved around survival is pleading for a household.
When God opens your eyes, you begin looking at the people you love differently.
You start thinking about your father.
Your daughter who wants nothing to do with church.
That person who laughs whenever you mention Jesus.
You begin praying differently because eternity is no longer theological vocabulary.
Rahab was told to place a scarlet cord in the window.
That cord would mark the house connected with the promise made to her.
We should be careful not to force every detail into symbolism Scripture itself does not explicitly establish. The text does not call the scarlet cord the blood of Christ.
But from where we stand in the completed biblical story, Rahab's rescue certainly makes us hunger for the greater rescue God ultimately provides through Jesus.
Because our hope is not a cord hanging from a window.
Our hope is Christ crucified and risen.
Our salvation rests not in our ability to hide ourselves from judgment but in the Savior who bore judgment for sinners and conquered death.
The walls that had seemed permanent were suddenly not permanent at all.
But Rahab and those gathered with her were brought out alive.
Joshua 6 records that Rahab and her family were spared because she had hidden the messengers.
The world she knew collapsing behind her.
Sometimes grace feels like being rescued from the very world you once thought you could not live without.
And then Scripture gives us a detail almost too beautiful to believe.
Rahab does not disappear from the biblical story.
And when Matthew opens his Gospel and begins tracing the human genealogy of Jesus the Messiah, there she is.
Matthew 1:5 names her in the family line that leads through Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David—and eventually to Jesus Christ.
Do you understand how staggering that is?
Jericho knew her as Rahab the prostitute.
Hebrews remembers her as a woman of faith.
James remembers faith expressed in action.
Matthew places her name in the Messiah's genealogy.
Scandal did not get the final word.
Her old identity was not erased by pretending it never existed.
It was overtaken by a greater story.
And perhaps that is why you are still reading.
Maybe there is something under the flax in your own life.
A wound you turned into a weapon.
A habit you promised God you would stop.
A prayer life that quietly died while everybody kept assuming you were spiritually strong.
You know how to keep people downstairs while the truth remains upstairs.
But Jesus already knows what is on the roof.
And still He calls sinners to come.
Repentance means we stop negotiating with the sin Christ died to save us from.
We bring it into His light.
And grace does not merely give us permission to remain what we were.
Rahab was not rescued so she could remain spiritually inside Jericho forever.
Maybe your Jericho is not a city.
Maybe it is the identity you refuse to release.
Maybe you have spent years saying:
But what if Jesus is calling you out?
What if the thing you call personality is actually bondage?
What if the secret you protect is the prison Christ is asking you to leave?
What if the shame telling you that you are too dirty for God is itself keeping you from the only One who can actually make you clean?
Jesus did not go to the cross for polished people pretending they never sinned.
He went to the cross because sinners needed a Savior.
People whose failures made headlines and people whose failures never left their bedrooms.
The ground at Calvary leaves no room for boasting.
Rahab reminds us that God can meet someone in a place nobody expects and begin writing a future nobody could predict.
What is still hiding under your flax?
What are you terrified Jesus will expose?
What if exposure before Christ is not the end of you?
What if confession is where hiding ends and healing begins?
If this touched something you have kept hidden, you do not need to tell strangers the details. But you can make one small confession of need.
And then look through those comments.
You may discover that the person beside you in the body of Christ is fighting harder than you knew.
Remind somebody that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It does not.
But if this biblical message can reach someone hiding behind shame, sharing it can become one simple act of witness.
There may be a Rahab on somebody's friends list tonight.
Someone convinced that his addiction has disqualified him.
Someone convinced her sexual past has permanently stained her.
Someone who thinks church is filled only with people who have always had their lives together.
Someone sitting alone wondering whether Jesus could possibly want them.
Then let Rahab point them beyond herself...
Because shame has a strange way of returning after the sermon ends.
There may come a night when your old name starts whispering again.
When your former life tries to reclaim you.
And Rahab's name eventually appeared in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Stay close for daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Christ.
Salvation cannot be purchased. God's favor cannot be bought.
But supporting Gospel Warrior can help us continue putting biblical teaching, Gospel-centered encouragement, and discipleship material in front of people who desperately need it.
Rahab's story is not ultimately about an impressive woman who reinvented herself.
It is about the astonishing mercy of God toward someone who believed Him.
And your story will not be redeemed by becoming impressive either.
Bring Him what happened ten years ago.
Bring Him what happened last night.
Bring Him the broken pieces you cannot put back together.
Because the hands pierced on Calvary are still better at writing endings than shame has ever been.
And maybe someday you will look backward and realize that the chapter you thought would destroy your entire story became the place where you finally discovered the God who could rewrite it.
Rahab hid two spies beneath stalks of flax.
God brought her out from behind Jericho's walls.
And generations later, when the genealogy of the Savior was written, her name was still there.
Not because sin did not matter.
Not because her past was imaginary.
The name shame tried to bury can become a testimony grace refuses to forget.
